analysis.one_liner: Bars health plans from gagging doctors and nurses about a patient's condition or treatment options.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 1996, referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: In the mid-1990s, some managed care plans and insurers wrote contract clauses that stopped doctors and nurses from telling patients about treatments the plan would not cover, or even discussing all their options. This bill would have made those clauses illegal, voided any that existed, and fined a plan up to $15,000 for each violation. States could still add their own rules as long as they were more protective. The bill never got past committee and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with private or public health coverage, who would be guaranteed that their doctors, nurses, and other licensed providers could freely discuss their condition and every treatment option without fear of contract penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in managed care and health plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any entity offering a health plan from including a provision that restricts a provider's communications with a patient about the patient's condition or treatment options, and voids any such provision already in a contract [S2][S3].
It backs the ban with a civil money penalty of up to $15,000 per violation, enforced through the same procedures used for Medicare fraud penalties [S3].

It covers all licensed providers — including nurse anesthetists and chiropractors — and applies to public and private plans, including employee benefit plans and their third-party administrators [S3].
States may keep or add their own rules on the same subject, but only if they are more protective of medical communications than this federal floor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans, which would lose the ability to write gag clauses into provider contracts — a tool for steering patients away from treatments the plan does not want to pay for and for limiting discussion of coverage limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

drawbacks.text: The bill only protects conversation, not care: a plan could still refuse to cover or restrict a treatment itself, so long as it does not restrict the doctor from discussing it [S3].

The carve-out in the bill lets plans require providers to participate in the plan's own quality-review programs and procedures, which critics of managed care argue can function much like the interference the bill bans [S3].

Enforcement is complaint-driven and penalties for oral restrictions only apply when they are part of a repeated pattern proven by a preponderance of the evidence, so an isolated verbal gag would rarely trigger a penalty [S3].

A good-faith objection from the plan side is that a uniform federal rule on private contract terms is broad, and plans argued they need review procedures to control costs; this bill answers that only partially, with a narrow quality-program exception [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real and direct — informed consent means little if a plan can silence the provider — while the cost falls on plans that lose one contracting tool, not on patients. The bill's honest weakness is that it protects what is said, not what is covered, so it is a narrow fix rather than a broad patients'-rights law. It was modestly drafted and never tested by debate or amendment because it never got a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on July 31, 1996, in the final months of the 104th Congress, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day; that referral is the last action ever recorded [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S1][S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans kept the ability to write communication-restricting clauses into provider contracts, since no federal ban took effect; patients gained nothing from this bill, though the gag-clause issue continued to draw attention in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health plans, which kept their gag clauses

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings that contract restrictions on physician disclosure violate informed consent, and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 1 Senate Democrat
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and only two senators were involved (both Democrats), so the partisan shape of support or opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would void the gag clauses these plans used in provider contracts to keep doctors from discussing treatments the plan would not cover. Their ability to control what patients hear is what the bill targets, and it is a cost patients otherwise bear directly.

industries.industry: Licensed health care providers (physicians, nurse anesthetists, chiropractors)
industries.note: Providers would be freed from contract provisions restricting what they may tell patients, strengthening their ability to meet informed-consent and ethical duties.
